articles.title: HJSC operating profit surges as container shipbuilding drives growth
articles.summary: HJ Shipbuilding & Construction (HJSC) reported a sharp increase in earnings for the first nine months of 2026, supported by stronger performance in its shipbuilding division and continued construction of high-value container vessels. The South Korean company recorded consolidated revenue of KRW 2.0044 trillion, up...
articles.body: HJ Shipbuilding & Construction (HJSC) reported a sharp increase in earnings for the first nine months of 2026, supported by stronger performance in its shipbuilding division and continued construction of high-value container vessels. The South Korean company recorded consolidated revenue of KRW 2.0044 trillion, up 46.3% from KRW 1.3701 trillion in the same period last year. Operating profit increased to KRW 155.4 billion from KRW 16.6 billion, while net income reached KRW 130.6 billion, compared with KRW 2.9 billion a year earlier. The results, disclosed in a regulatory filing on 12 November, extend the improvement recorded during the first half of 2026. Container shipbuilding supports stronger profitability HJSC attributed much of its earnings growth to improved profitability in its shipbuilding division, which includes commercial and special-purpose vessels. Construction of environmentally friendly, high-value container ships gained momentum during the reporting period, contributing to higher revenue and stronger margins. The shipbuilding division generated revenue of KRW 1.1297 trillion, an increase of 88.1% from KRW 600.5 billion in the first nine months of 2025. Its operating profit reached KRW 149.7 billion, accounting for most of the group’s total operating earnings. Special-purpose ship projects, including maintenance, repair and overhaul work for the US Navy, also supported the division’s financial performance. According to HJSC, increased dock utilisation and improvements in production efficiency helped maintain operations despite fewer working days during the summer and Chuseok holiday periods. Meanwhile, the construction division reported revenue of KRW 874.2 billion and operating profit of KRW 5.6 billion. The division continued to benefit from public-sector construction, civil engineering and housing projects. “The increased share of revenue from high-value-added vessels and various special-purpose ship projects in the shipbuilding division, along with stable order wins and business operations in the construction division, contributed to our strong performance,” said an HJSC official. Looking ahead, HJSC plans to maintain its focus on profitability across both divisions. The company intends to improve its competitiveness in shipbuilding while pursuing selective construction contracts and tighter project cost management.

articles.title: Vestas CEO Calls For EU Crackdown on Chinese Software Used in Wind Sector
articles.summary: As the European Union weighs tougher cybersecurity rules, it should consider a ban on Chinese components and technology containing software in critical energy infrastructure, the CEO of Danish wind turbine maker Vestas told Reuters."When it comes to critical infrastructure…
articles.body: Vestas CEO Calls For EU Crackdown on Chinese Software Used in Wind Sector Maritime Activity Reports, Inc. November 17, 2026 © Adobe Stock/Peter Adams As the European Union weighs tougher cybersecurity rules, it should consider a ban on Chinese components and technology containing software in critical energy infrastructure, the CEO of Danish wind turbine maker Vestas told Reuters. "When it comes to critical infrastructure, meaning technology or components that has a software element in it, I think we should have a very upfront 'no thank you'," CEO Henrik Andersen said when asked whether Europe should adopt rules similar to China’s restrictions on foreign technology. "The energy assets you build now last 30 to 50 years, and you have to make sure you can control them yourself," he said. The European Union is revising its cybersecurity rules and requirements for European-made equipment while governments expand their power grids to handle increased renewable energy supply. China's commerce ministry has said it would take strong countermeasures if the bloc adopts the revised Cybersecurity Act proposed in January, arguing the law would abandon technological neutrality and undermine China-EU trade. Chinese manufacturers supplied a fraction of Europe's new turbines last year but are pushing to enter the market. Vestas' Andersen said the EU should require that about half of its wind assets are made in Europe, and that a turbine’s control systems and software should be treated separately from that requirement. A German developer dropped China's Ming Yang from a North Sea project last year. Britain said in March it would not support the use of turbines from China's Ming Yang in UK offshore wind on security grounds. Ming Yang in a statement to Reuters on Monday said it stores all turbine data locally in Europe, that operators retain full control, and that no remote access is permitted without the operator's explicit approval. CHINA HAS ALSO TIGHTENED RULES Andersen noted that Chinese authorities have imposed similar rules, telling Vestas that it could no longer monitor the sensors on its own turbines or update its turbines' software remotely from Europe, on the grounds that foreign access posed a risk to China's grid. "China put a marker in the sand five years ago, and now it's time that we say that marker counts on both sides," Andersen told Reuters at the company's headquarters in Copenhagen. Chinese utilities are replacing Western equipment with domestic alternatives, Poland's state-funded Centre for Eastern Studies said in a report last month. Andersen, whose company stands to gain if Chinese rivals are kept out of Europe, said he did not support a blanket ban on Chinese components but that if Europe believed in free competition, Vestas should have the same access to China's market, which it no longer has. "If we are going to play football, then let's play football. Eleven a side and a referee in the middle," he said. He said attacks that cranked up fridge temperatures at supermarkets across Europe this month were a reminder that whoever holds the software updates controls the machine, whether it is a refrigerator, car or wind turbine. While no one has claimed responsibility for those attacks, they have heightened concerns among European authorities about hybrid threats to infrastructure. "There is a security risk if you are not the one holding the username, password and access," Andersen said. Ming Yang in the written statement said it also supported cybersecurity rules being applied equally to every supplier, but added that supplier-specific assessment and verifiable safeguards were preferable to "blanket exclusions based on country of origin". The China Chamber of Commerce to the EU and China’s commerce ministry did not respond to requests for comment. (Reuters)

articles.title: Gulf Oil Flow at Risk From Lack of Empty Tankers, Tracker Says
articles.summary: The number of empty tankers sailing to collect cargoes of Middle East crude is sliding, a trend that could jeopardize the recent revival in the region’s oil flows to global markets, according to Tankertrackers.com, a firm that monitors vessel movements.

Join the leading maritime news network Stock Photo: Faraways/Shutterstock By Alaric Nightingale (Bloomberg) — The number of empty tankers sailing to collect cargoes of Middle East crude is sliding, a trend that could jeopardize the recent revival in the region’s oil flows to global markets, according to Tankertrackers.com, a firm that monitors vessel movements. The industry uses two main ship types to get oil from the Persian Gulf to the world: very large crude carriers, which transport 2 million-barrel cargoes, and Suezmaxes that move about half that. The collective capacity of those vessels sailing empty to the region has declined by about 40% since the end of August, according to Tankertrackers.com figures. While the market is intensely focused on how much oil leaves the Middle East, those flows are only possible if there’s a steady stream of ships arriving to pick up the barrels. The Iran war has meant that some vessels refuse to go through the Strait of Hormuz, instead receiving cargoes in locations like the Gulf of Oman from tankers that are willing to risk shuttling through the crucial waterway. There are “not enough vacant tankers to take oil out of the region,” Tankertrackers.com’s co-founder, Samir Madani, said by WhatsApp. “It’s one thing to bring the oil out into the Gulf of Oman via the Strait of Hormuz, but it seems like there isn’t enough to take the oil out of the Gulf of Oman.” In broad terms, there has been a dip in flows from the region at large so far this month, though it’s still unclear what the causes of the drop are, the exact scale of the decrease, or how long-lasting the decline will be, Madani said. For now, though, the number of ships transferring cargoes onto other ships outside the Persian Gulf remains high, enabling shipments toward customers to continue for the time being, he said. Oil tanker rates have declined from record levels over the past few weeks, helping to reduce the cost of delivering crude to customers. Any shortage in the number of empty vessels would support rates. Iran has attacked shipping consistently throughout the conflict, something that has deterred transits. The number of incidents reported officially jumped last month, and remains at high levels so far in November, according to data from the International Maritime Organization and the UK Maritime Trade Operations Centre. © 2026 Bloomberg L.P. articles.title: NTSB Warned of Mississippi River Passenger Vessel Collision Risks Nearly 30 Years Ago
articles.summary: Nearly three decades before a tanker slammed into a docked river cruise ship in New Orleans, the National Transportation Safety Board warned that passenger vessels along the Mississippi River waterfront...

The accident prompted NTSB safety recommendations addressing the risks posed by large commercial vessels to passenger ships docked along the Mississippi River. (Image: NTSB accident investigation report) Nearly three decades before a tanker slammed into a docked river cruise ship in New Orleans, the National Transportation Safety Board warned that passenger vessels along the Mississippi River waterfront were vulnerable to being struck by large commercial ships and urged authorities to consider relocating them or installing protective measures. The warning came in a 1998 NTSB investigation into the Bright Field accident, when a Liberian-flagged bulk carrier lost propulsion and crashed into the New Orleans riverfront, injuring 62 people. Now, the findings are drawing renewed attention following Friday’s allision between the Marshall Islands-flagged tanker Atlantic Asphalt and American Cruise Lines’ American Heritage , which capsized after being struck while docked near the Crescent City Connection Bridge right in the heart of downtown New Orleans. All 190 passengers and crew aboard the riverboat survived the November 13 accident, although 32 people were taken to hospitals. The similarities between the two accidents are striking, particularly because the earlier investigation specifically identified the dangers facing passenger vessels moored along the busy commercial waterway. In its report on the December 14, 1996, Bright Field accident, the NTSB concluded that the Coast Guard, Port of New Orleans and waterfront operators had failed to adequately assess, manage or mitigate the risks of locating unprotected commercial facilities in areas vulnerable to vessel strikes. Notably, the Bright Field stopped just 70 feet from the docked gaming vessel Queen of New Orleans , while its bow wave caused the gangway of the nearby paddlewheeler Creole Queen to collapse, sending three passengers into the Mississippi River. The Creole Queen had 190 passengers and crew aboard — the same approximate number reported aboard American Heritage during Friday’s collision. The NTSB subsequently criticized the vessels’ emergency evacuation arrangements and issued additional safety recommendations. In its report, the agency issued two recommendations addressing the placement of passenger vessels along the river. Recommendation M-98-1 directed the Coast Guard, working with the Port of New Orleans, to reassess the risks of passenger vessel berths along the Mississippi River’s left descending bank and determine whether vessels should be moved to safer locations or protected through procedural, operational or physical barriers. Another recommendation, M-98-10, directed the Port of New Orleans to undertake the same assessment in cooperation with the Coast Guard. The NTSB also called for a comprehensive risk assessment of maritime and shoreside activities throughout the port, including measures to reduce the dangers associated with commercial vessel traffic. In that earlier investigation, the NTSB highlighted the risks created by large vessels navigating the narrow, heavily trafficked river near passenger terminals, commercial developments and other vulnerable infrastructure, and identified potential mitigation measures including reduced vessel speeds, tug escorts and moving passenger vessels to safer locations. The danger of mechanical failure was also well documented. When the Coast Guard subsequently finalized additional Lower Mississippi River navigation regulations in 1999, it noted that more than 300 self-propelled vessels of at least 1,600 gross tons had experienced propulsion losses, steering casualties or engine irregularities on the Mississippi River during 1995 and 1996. The 1999 regulations established additional operating requirements for larger commercial vessels and required certain passenger vessels moored or anchored in the river to maintain manned pilothouse watches and monitor emergency communications. Those requirements, now contained in 33 CFR 165.810 , were intended to improve navigation safety and allow passenger vessel crews to respond quickly to emergencies. The regulatory action demonstrates that authorities did respond to the earlier accident. However, the extent to which the NTSB’s separate recommendations concerning passenger vessel placement and protective barriers were implemented at individual berths remains unclear. The current official disposition of recommendations M-98-1 and M-98-10 has not been independently confirmed. Nor has it been established what specific risk assessments or protective measures were in place at the berth occupied by American Heritage . Those questions could become significant as investigators examine the circumstances surrounding Friday’s collision. According to the NTSB’s ongoing investigation , the Atlantic Asphalt was traveling upriver near the Crescent City Connection Bridge when it experienced what investigators described as a steering casualty. Preliminary information recovered from the tanker’s voyage data recorder indicates the vessel’s rudder remained in a starboard position, causing the tanker to veer toward the river’s east bank. Approximately two minutes later, the tanker struck American Heritage at its berth. The riverboat subsequently overturned, forcing passengers and crew to evacuate as emergency responders and nearby commercial vessels rushed to assist. Investigators have not determined what caused the steering failure. While the Bright Field accident involved a loss of propulsion rather than steering, both incidents demonstrate the consequences of a large commercial vessel losing maneuvering capability in the confined waters of downtown New Orleans. The NTSB has not determined whether the location of the American Heritage berth or the protective measures in place contributed to Friday’s accident. Nor is there evidence at this stage that either vessel or port authorities violated the regulations adopted following the earlier casualty. But the 1998 recommendations raise an important question nearly 30 years after federal investigators identified the danger of large commercial ships striking passenger vessels along the New Orleans waterfront. For the NTSB, which has repeatedly warned across transportation sectors about the dangers of leaving identified safety risks unresolved, the latest collision presents another opportunity to examine whether lessons from an earlier accident could have made a difference in this latest case. articles.title: Hapag-Lloyd expands Asia-Latin America network with two new standalone services
articles.summary: Hapag-Lloyd is further strengthening its network between Asia and Latin America with the introduction of two new standalone services in 2027. The Asia-Mexico Express (AMX) and Asia-South America Express (ASX) will complement the company’s existing AN1, AN2, TPM and AS3 services, providing customers with broader...
articles.body: Hapag-Lloyd expands Asia-Latin America network with two new standalone services in International Shipping News 17/11/2026 Hapag-Lloyd is further strengthening its network between Asia and Latin America with the introduction of two new standalone services in 2027. The Asia-Mexico Express (AMX) and Asia-South America Express (ASX) will complement the company’s existing AN1, AN2, TPM and AS3 services, providing customers with broader network coverage, additional routing options and greater flexibility. The Asia-Mexico Express (AMX) will launch in January 2027, offering weekly sailings between Asia and Mexico with Panamax-class vessels and onward connections along the West Coast of Latin America. The Asia-South America Express (ASX) will follow in April 2027, connecting Asia with the East Coast of South America, including the River Plate region. Vessels with capacities ranging from 6,000 to 8,000 TEU will be deployed on this service. “Latin America is an important market for Hapag-Lloyd, with significant opportunities for further growth. By complementing our existing services with two independently operated connections, we are strengthening our overall network offering and providing our customers with more choice, flexibility and reliable transport solutions,” says Esteban Perez, Senior Director Trade Management Latin America at Hapag-Lloyd. articles.body: Noatum CSM expands regional client base and managed fleet in first year of operations in International Shipping News 17/11/2026 Noatum CSM has expanded its managed fleet and secured new regional clients during its first year of operations, strengthening its position in the Middle East’s growing shipmanagement sector. The joint venture between AD Ports Group and Columbia Shipmanagement celebrated its first anniversary at an event in the UAE this month attended by clients, partners and senior maritime executives, highlighting its progress in establishing UAE as a hub for international shipmanagement services The anniversary comes amid continuing geopolitical uncertainty affecting international shipping, with disruption across major trading corridors placing additional pressure on vessel operators and their crews. Xanthos Kyriacou, CEO of Noatum CSM, said: “One year ago, we set sail with a clear vision, ambitious targets and a strong belief in what we would achieve. Today, I’m proud of how far we have come and grateful to everyone who has been part of this journey. “Since then, we have strengthened our operations, expanded our fleet, welcomed new clients and laid a solid foundation for sustainable growth,” he added. Noatum CSM held an event to mark its first anniversary since officially launching The company’s development reflects increasing demand for shipmanagement expertise in the Middle East, as regional shipowners seek high-quality technical management, operational efficiency and internationally recognised standards. Since launching operations, Noatum CSM has strengthened its technical and operational capabilities, expanded its portfolio and built relationships with shipowners across the region. Andreas Hadjipetrou, CEO of Columbia Group was in attendance at the event and while addressing guests said the joint venture had already delivered on its original objectives of strengthening management services for AD Ports Group while attracting additional business. He said: “The objective was to build a world-class shipmanagement company in the region, and we are already seeing this becoming a reality. We have welcomed many new clients, and the company is performing better than planned. Our ambition is to become the trusted ship management leader in the region, and we are very pleased with the growth so far. “ Xanthos Kyriacou, CEO of Noatum CSM addressing guests at the event Discussing the conflict in the Middle East, Mr Kyriacou emphasised that protecting seafarers remains central to the company’s approach. “In moments like this, our first responsibility is the safety and wellbeing of our seafarers who serve on our vessels, and I want to underline that this is on top of our agenda. It is in demanding times that the value of a responsible, well-prepared ship manager is demonstrated, and we remain committed to being exactly that,” he said. Looking ahead, Noatum CSM intends to continue investing in its people, developing its operational capabilities and embracing innovation as it strengthens its position in the regional and international shipmanagement markets. “Our first year has been a strong beginning, but there is much, much more to achieve, and I’m confident that the best is yet to come,” Mr Kyriacou added. Iran’s Revolutionary Guards Navy warned shipping companies against using the U.S.-backed southern route through the Strait of Hormuz, describing it as fully closed and a “minefield of fire,” according to regional media outlets citing a statement from the force. Brig. Gen. Mohammad Akrami-Nia, a spokesperson for the Iranian Army, said the Strait of Hormuz would not reopen until “the enemy accepts Iran’s conditions.” Separately, CNN reported Monday that new U.S. intelligence indicated Iran was developing plans that could target senior Trump administration officials with a so-called dirty bomb, or a chemical weapon in Washington, D.C. CNBC cannot immediately verify the report. The intelligence was characterized as an effort by Iran to develop options rather than evidence of an imminent attack, CNN reported. U.S. officials have held several meetings over the past week to consider how to respond to the potential threat. The heightened security concerns come after Iranian threats prompted Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent to relocate to military housing last week. “We remain vigilant, monitoring any and all potential threats, but at this time there are no credible threats to the homeland,” a White House spokesperson said in a statement to CNBC. Oil prices inched lower in Asian trading Tuesday, with international benchmark Brent crude futures dropping 0.7% to $91.8 a barrel and U.S. West Texas Intermediate futures falling 0.7% to $85.1 a barrel. War escalation looms On Tuesday, the U.K. Maritime Trade Operations said a tanker was struck by an unidentified projectile in the Strait of Hormuz and subsequently caught fire. The agency did not say who was responsible and urged vessels to transit with caution and report suspicious activity. Separately, the Iranian navy said four oil tankers had struck mines and caught fire in the eastern Strait of Hormuz over the previous 24 hours. The escalation in Tehran’s rhetoric came as the USS Theodore Roosevelt arrived in the Gulf region on Sunday, joining the USS George H.W. Bush and USS George Washington. That added to U.S. firepower near Iran even as President Donald Trump said the war was winding down. Trump has sent mixed signals regarding the conflict in recent weeks, alternating between declaring it could soon end and warning of renewed large-scale strikes if efforts to reach a deal fail. After meeting Qatari Prime Minister Sheikh Mohammed bin Abdulrahman Al Thani last week, Trump said the war with Iran could end “fairly soon,” adding that it “militarily is effectively over.” Tehran said Sunday that it launched six drones at a U.S. air-defense radar at Bahrain’s Riffa air base, the second attack Iran claimed against the kingdom in three days. Bahrain’s military said it intercepted and destroyed several Iranian aerial attacks. Secretary of State Marco Rubio condemned the attacks in a call Monday with Bahraini Foreign Minister Abdullatif bin Rashid Al Zayani and reaffirmed Washington’s commitment to the security of Bahrain and other Gulf partners. The conflict began in late February when the U.S. and Israel attacked Iran, prompting Tehran to retaliate with strikes on Israel and Gulf states hosting American military bases. Indirect talks between Washington and Tehran through Qatar have since appeared to run into a stalemate as warring powers disagreed over terms to reach a lasting peace deal. ‘Misread’ of Iran’s resistance Washington appears unwilling to accept several of Iran’s demands to end the war, including lifting the U.S. naval blockade on its southern ports and lifting sanctions, while stressing that Iran cannot possess a nuclear weapon. Iran is likely to continue escalating attacks on tankers and container ships, along with occasional strikes on U.S. military targets, in an effort to pressure Washington into offering concessions, said Ian Bremmer, president and founder of Eurasia Group. In response, Washington will likely expand its blockade on Iran’s maritime and inland trade routes, he said. “The presumption is that eventually Iran can’t handle the economic pressure and will accept better terms,” Bremmer said, calling that view a “misread of the Iranian leadership and their capacity to resist.” Over the coming year, Iran is likely to intensify efforts to disrupt shipping through the Strait of Hormuz, Bremmer said. articles.body: Contractor appointed for Port of Gothenburg fairway deepening project in Port News 17/11/2026 The Swedish Maritime Administration has awarded a joint venture between Boskalis Sweden AB, Van Oord Sweden AB and Rohde Nielsen A/S the contract to deepen and widen the fairway to the Port of Gothenburg. The award is an important step in the Skandia Gateway project, which will make it possible to receive today’s largest container vessels fully laden, as well as even larger vessels in the future. “It is very gratifying that the project is now moving forward according to plan. Cargo volumes in the port are increasing, vessels are operating at greater draft, and the long-term congestion in other major European ports means that the fairway deepening continues to be of the utmost strategic importance,” says Elin Dörrheide, Project Manager for Skandia Gateway at the Port of Gothenburg. The Port of Gothenburg is the largest port in the Nordic region and a central link between Swedish industry and the global market. Today, the depth of the fairway limits how much cargo the largest container vessels can transport to and from Gothenburg. The Skandia Gateway project includes deepening and widening the fairway as well as adaptations to the quay and port basin. The Skandia Gateway project includes deepening and widening the fairway as well as adaptations to the quay and port basin. “Shipping is crucial for Swedish industry and trade. With the planned measures in the Skandia Gateway project, the largest container vessels will be able to transport more cargo to and from Gothenburg. This strengthens business access to efficient maritime transport and Sweden’s competitiveness,” says Thomas Nord, Head of Unit at the Swedish Maritime Administration. The contract includes dredging approximately 7 million cubic metres of loose dredged material and rock, as well as adapting the fairway markings. This makes Skandia Gateway one of the largest dredging projects in Sweden. Work on the fairway is planned to start in August 2027, and the entire project is expected to be completed in autumn 2028. At that point, the Port of Gothenburg will be able to receive vessels with a draft of 16.5 metres, compared with today’s 13.5 metres. Through an option in the contract, the Port of Gothenburg has the possibility of ordering additional deepening in order to accommodate vessels with a draft of up to 17.5 metres. “This is a very important milestone in one of Sweden’s largest fairway projects. After many years of studies, environmental permit processes and optimisation of the fairway design, we are now looking forward to moving ahead with implementation,” says Jenny Röström Wicander, Project Manager for Skandia Gateway at the Swedish Maritime Administration. After the previous procurement was cancelled in autumn 2025, the project optimized the fairway design and reduced the scope of dredging. At the same time, quayside work has continued under the management of the Port of Gothenurg. The quay reinforcement has been completed and a separate dredging work close to the quay is now underway. The contract value for the base assignment amounts to approximately SEK 2.3 billion, with the possibility of calling off additional work through agreed options. The contract is planned to be signed at the end of 2026 between the Swedish Maritime Administration, Gothenburg Port Authority and a joint venture between Boskalis Sweden AB, Van Oord Sweden AB and Rohde Nielsen A/S, provided that the award decision is not subject to legal challenge. articles.body: DP World Cuts 50,000 Tonnes Of UK Freight Emissions With Rail Programme in Port News 17/11/2026 Three years after launching a pioneering Modal Shift Programme at Southampton, DP World has helped avoid an estimated 50,000 tonnes of CO₂e emissions by encouraging cargo owners to shift from road to rail. This financial incentive scheme has helped move more than 220,000 additional containers by rail from DP World Southampton since its launch in 2023, avoiding an estimated 18 million miles of road transport. The programme has also helped increase rail’s share of container movements from Southampton from 21% to 29%, while supporting the introduction of five new rail services connecting the port to Birmingham, Cardiff, East Midlands Gateway, Doncaster and Northampton. Together, these developments are strengthening rail connectivity at the UK’s third-largest container port, giving customers greater choice in how they move goods inland. Kris Adams, CEO, UK Ports and Terminals, at DP World, said: “Decarbonising supply chains requires practical solutions that make commercial sense for customers. Our Modal Shift Programme shows what can be achieved when we work with our partners to make lower-emission transport options more accessible and attractive. “Too often, the conversation around supply chain decarbonisation pits rail against road, but the Modal Shift Programme shows how DP World is using bespoke trials that work to deliver on both sides of UK supply chains. We’re delighted with the success of the trial and look forward to new opportunities to expand it further across our operations in the UK.” Building on the programme’s success, DP World is now expanding its incentive structure to include Rail Freight Terminal Operators (RFTOs), creating new opportunities to increase rail freight volumes from Southampton. Under the new arrangements, eligible operators will be able to receive performance-based disbursements for each import laden-container moved by rail within the programme’s incentive zone, subject to meeting quarterly targets. Originally launched as a six-month trial in 2023, the Modal Shift Programme provides financial incentives to customers moving import-laden containers by rail from Southampton to destinations within 140 miles of the railhead. articles.body: The Board of Commissioners of the Port Authority of New York and New Jersey has approved a request to advance plans to replace the central heating and refrigeration plant serving Terminals A, B and C at Newark Liberty International Airport. The work may include planning for phased construction at operating facilities and other projects, together with expenses linked to procuring construction awards. The new plant is intended to be a foundational part of the airport’s modernisation, supplying heating, cooling and potentially power to more than 5 million square feet of existing and future terminal space. The existing plant was built in 1973 and is nearing the end of its useful life. Its current site cannot house the larger facility needed to serve the new and expanded terminals envisaged in the EWR Vision Plan, and the Port Authority’s 2026-2035 Capital Plan includes funds for its replacement. The project is expected to be delivered in phases while maintaining passenger service in all terminals, and to include sustainability measures aligned with the agency’s net-zero roadmap. Alongside the Board’s decision, the Port Authority issued a nonbinding Request for Expressions of Interest to identify firms interested in the future procurement and to gather market feedback on commercial structure, technical delivery, phasing, performance management, decarbonisation and future-proofing. It is particularly seeking responses from infrastructure equity investors, developers, energy-as-a-service providers, operators, financial institutions, designers and builders with experience of complex energy and aviation infrastructure. A competitive, transparent procurement is intended to follow. Under the proposed framework, the selected developer would design, build, finance, operate and maintain the plant and its distribution infrastructure, and would work with, and potentially contract with, airport energy users including terminal operators, airlines and other tenants. The plant forms part of the wider transformation of Newark Liberty that began with the opening of Terminal A in 2023, which won the 2024 World’s Best New Airport Terminal award and a five-star Skytrax rating. A new AirTrain Newark is under construction, planning and design are under way for a new Terminal B, and a new entry point to the airport’s rail station is being built to improve access to NJ TRANSIT and Amtrak’s Northeast Corridor services. Chairman Kevin O’Toole said the investments so far have begun a generational transformation of the airport. Executive Director Kathryn Garcia said the request for expressions of interest helps turn the EWR Vision Plan into reality and is an invitation to invest not only in Newark Airport but in New Jersey itself.

The talks are aimed at "bridging perspectives and narrowing the gap between proposals presented on the ground," Qatari spokesperson Majed Al Ansari said. They coincide with a visit to Oman by Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araqchi. Oman's Foreign Ministry said he discussed safeguarding maritime corridors and ensuring the smooth flow of global shipping and trade, as well as preventing military escalation, with Oman's foreign minister. Oman and Iran lie on opposite sides of the Strait of Hormuz, a vital waterway that carried about one-fifth of global oil and liquefied natural gas supplies before the war but is now partly blocked by Iran. Oman has previously held talks with Tehran about controlling traffic in the Strait of Hormuz. Araqchi said in a post on Telegram that he also met Oman's Sultan Haitham ‌bin Tariq and informed him about Iran's diplomatic initiative to end the war that began with US and Israeli strikes on Iran on February 28. RISE IN ATTACKS ON TANKERS The war has ground to a stalemate, with US President Donald Trump saying he might hold off from attacking Iran if the US does not face what he described as provocations from Tehran or the Iran-backed Houthi group in Yemen. Trump said on Tuesday the US was taking seriously the possibility that Iran could be ‌planning an attack involving a so-called dirty bomb in Washington, after being asked about a CNN report citing US intelligence assessments. Iran's foreign ministry spokesperson said the report was part of a US campaign "to lay the media groundwork for their sinister designs" using "baseless allegations". Trump has also said he will maintain a US naval blockade on Iran because it has continued to disrupt shipping in the Strait of Hormuz, which is a sticking point in negotiations. Attacks on tankers have increased this month in the strait, and the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations agency said the crew of a tanker passing through the waterway was unaccounted for after being attacked north of ⁠the Omani port city of Khasab. Iran's Revolutionary Guards and navy said on Tuesday that a ship carrying LNG and two oil tankers had caught fire in the strait. Reuters could not independently verify the reports. Benchmark Brent crude futures were up 0.4% at $92.76 a barrel on Tuesday, much higher than before the war but well below April's wartime peak of $126.41. IRANIAN WARNING The war also continues to spill over into other parts of the Middle East as Iran puts pressure on Washington through its Houthi allies, who have carried out attacks on Saudi Arabia and seized areas along the Yemeni coast on the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, hoping to squeeze Gulf oil producers. Tuesday's attack on Bahrain, a Shi'ite-majority country ruled by a Sunni Muslim family, followed the sentencing there of 64 people, mostly Shi'ite clerics, to life in prison on charges of colluding with Iran to undermine the state. Iran's foreign ministry condemned the court's ruling on Tuesday and said the accusations were baseless. Tehran has long denied interference in Bahrain's internal affairs. Iran also fired on Bahrain two days ago,saying it had targeted a US radar system at the Al-Rifaa helicopter base following what it said were hostile US actions. Iran's Revolutionary Guards spokesperson said Bahrain had made "three key mistakes", which he listed as "cooperating in the invasion of the Islamic Republic of Iran, remaining within the US security bubble, and encroaching on the sanctity of Shi'ite religious authority". These, "if continued, will jeopardize its survival in the region's new security order," ⁠Hossein Mohebbi said. (Reuters)

articles.summary: Norway is moving a step closer to testing nuclear propulsion for commercial ships, with a consortium including shipbuilder VARD and offshore vessel operator Island Offshore securing NOK 20 million ($2...

VARD/Island Offshore Norway is moving a step closer to testing nuclear propulsion for commercial ships, with a consortium including shipbuilder VARD and offshore vessel operator Island Offshore securing NOK 20 million ($2 million) in government funding to develop an integrated nuclear power system for offshore vessels. The Marine Nuclear Propulsion System (MarNuPS) project , led by Emerald Nuclear Norway, aims to move the technology from engineering studies into full-scale testing, with a first vessel deployment targeted for 2031 or 2032. The initial funding comes from the Research Council of Norway and supports a broader development program that will bring together reactor technology, ship design, electrical systems and vessel operations. The first phase, scheduled for 2027, will establish a test facility at Stette, near Ålesund, where the partners plan to assemble and test a full-scale representation of the proposed shipboard propulsion system. Importantly, the initial testing will not involve an operating nuclear reactor. Instead, the system will use electric heating to simulate the reactor’s thermal output, allowing engineers to evaluate how the propulsion and power systems work together before moving to nuclear operation. Testing will examine normal vessel operations, rapid changes in power demand, system performance, stress conditions and crew interaction. The project is based on Emerald Nuclear’s 5-megawatt-electric GEM Microreactor technology, using a gas-cooled reactor design coupled with a supercritical carbon dioxide turbine system to generate electricity. The integrated system will also include energy storage, remote monitoring, power management and shipboard automation. According to Emerald Nuclear , the first phase has an estimated total cost of NOK 150 million ($15.6 million), with project partners providing substantial funding beyond the government grant. For VARD, part of Italy’s Fincantieri Group, the project represents another step toward bringing advanced nuclear technology into commercial shipbuilding. Its subsidiary Vard Electro will focus on integrating the power system with the electrical controls and automation systems used aboard ships. “We also view this funding award as a vital sign of national support for nuclear applications in maritime going forward,” said Håvard Vollset Lien, Vice President of Research and Innovation at Vard Group. Island Offshore, meanwhile, hopes to become the first offshore service vessel operator to install the system. “Nuclear energy has the potential to provide a new route to decarbonising offshore vessels without compromising the power, endurance and operational flexibility these ships require,” said Tommy Walaunet, CEO of Island Offshore. Emerald Nuclear is also proposing a different commercial model for shipboard nuclear power. Rather than requiring shipowners to purchase and operate reactors themselves, the company would retain ownership and operational responsibility, including maintenance and nuclear fuel management. Shipowners would instead pay for the electricity they use. The consortium also includes the Norwegian University of Science and Technology (NTNU), Imperial College London and engineering specialist Maskindynamikk, bringing together expertise in nuclear modelling, structural integrity, monitoring and marine operations. The project builds on Norway’s earlier NuProShip research initiatives, which have examined the feasibility of nuclear propulsion for commercial shipping. While significant technical testing, safety validation and regulatory work remain before the technology can be deployed at sea, the next phase will provide an early full-scale demonstration of how a nuclear energy system could be integrated into an offshore vessel. articles.body: The Port of Oakland and Everport Terminal Services, marked the arrival of new electric cargo-handling equipment at the Oakland Seaport. Everport has invested in eight battery-electric top picks, heavy-duty machines that stack containers weighing up to 100,000 pounds and load them onto trucks, a role historically filled by diesel equipment. The machines are American-made Taylor Machine Works ZLC996 electric container handlers, each expected to run two full shifts on a single charge. ETS funded the purchase privately. The arrival follows another step in October, when the port began construction of infrastructure improvements to convert the Matson Terminal to 100 percent zero-emissions operations. That work is part of a US$ 119 million investment from the Port and Freight Infrastructure Program, funded by the California State Transportation Agency. Together, the projects support the port’s goals of greater competitiveness, improved freight efficiency and lower emissions, in line with California’s wider clean transportation objectives. Ron Neal, President of Everport Terminal Services, said the company is committed to an efficient and sustainable operation, and called the investment an important step toward zero-emission cargo handling and modernising the terminal for the next generation. Port of Oakland Executive Director Kristi McKenney described the milestone as part of a journey toward zero emissions begun many years ago with many partners, and said the mix of public and private investment in US-made electric equipment creates jobs at the port and in towns across the country.

(Photo: Hanwha Defense USA) South Korea’s Hanwha Aerospace and its U.S. subsidiary have successfully test-fired a Chunmoo guided missile from a vessel off the Mississippi coast, marking another step toward deploying precision-strike weapons aboard crewed and unmanned naval vessels. The launch took place Sunday, November 15, aboard a test-range vessel operated by Mississippi-based The Spaceport Company , using a palletized launcher designed to be installed on maritime platforms. According to Hanwha Defense USA, the firing completed a two-launch test campaign aimed at validating the Chunmoo missile system for operations at sea. The tests also evaluated the launcher and its electronics as the company works to develop a maritime strike capability that could be deployed across different classes of vessels. The effort comes as the U.S. Navy looks to expand its use of distributed maritime strike systems, including weapons carried aboard smaller warships and unmanned surface vessels. “Hanwha is answering the U.S. Navy’s call to produce and field modern strike capabilities from a maritime platform,” said Kevin Schoonover, executive vice president for missiles at Hanwha Defense USA. “By pairing Hanwha’s flagship Chunmoo missile and its palletized platform with next generation crewed and uncrewed vessels, we can deliver capabilities for the Navy at scale and a fraction of the cost of other systems.” Schoonover said data collected during the tests would help guide future development of palletized and containerized launch systems for distributed maritime operations and expeditionary strike missions. Unlike permanently installed missile launchers, palletized and containerized systems are designed to provide greater flexibility in how weapons are integrated aboard ships, potentially allowing a wider range of vessels to carry precision-strike capabilities. The demonstration also involved Magnet Defense, which deployed its research vessel to track and evaluate the missile launch. Hanwha Defense USA and Magnet Defense announced a strategic partnership in April to develop and produce medium unmanned surface vessels for the U.S. military. The partnership includes plans for a 38-meter unmanned vessel and the integration of advanced weapons and autonomous systems. The latest missile test could help advance those efforts, although Hanwha has not announced a timetable for operational deployment of the ship-based Chunmoo system. The Spaceport Company, which specializes in offshore launch operations, has conducted more than 10 launches using mobile launch vessels, barges and semi-submersible platforms. Hanwha said its testing program will continue to gather technical and operational data to support the development of maritime strike capabilities for future naval and expeditionary operations. articles.title: Study: Connecting Great Lakes, Inland Waterways Could Deliver Millions in Freight Savings
articles.summary: A new study commissioned by the American Great Lakes Ports Association (AGLPA) identifies opportunities to expand freight movements between the Great Lakes and U.S. inland waterways, potentially delivering millions of dollars in transportation…
articles.body: Study: Connecting Great Lakes, Inland Waterways Could Deliver Millions in Freight Savings Maritime Activity Reports, Inc. November 17, 2026 Copyright Reimar/AdobeStock A new study commissioned by the American Great Lakes Ports Association (AGLPA) identifies opportunities to expand freight movements between the Great Lakes and U.S. inland waterways, potentially delivering millions of dollars in transportation savings while improving supply chain flexibility and making better use of existing maritime infrastructure. Released November 17, The Great Freight Connection, prepared by transportation consultancy CPCS Transcom Inc., examines existing freight movements between the two systems and evaluates four potential trade corridors involving Port Milwaukee, Ports of Indiana–Burns Harbor and the Illinois International Port District. The findings reveal a significant disconnect between two of America's most important freight networks. In 2023, more than 138 million tons of cargo moved on the Great Lakes and Illinois Waterway systems, yet less than 1% of outbound Great Lakes tonnage moved to the Illinois Waterway. Conversely, approximately 5% of outbound Illinois Waterway cargo moved toward the Great Lakes. Despite their physical connection through Chicago, the systems largely function as separate freight networks. Putting Numbers to the Opportunity The study evaluates four representative trade lanes: grain shipments from Milwaukee to the Gulf Coast, steel from Burns Harbor to Peoria and St. Louis, liquid bulk from Joliet to Milwaukee, and salt moving north from the Gulf to Chicago. Among the most promising opportunities is steel transportation from Burns Harbor to inland markets. The study estimates potential savings of approximately $20.70 per ton for shipments to Peoria and $34.40 per ton to St. Louis compared with trucking. At an illustrative annual volume of 100,000 tons, those savings could reach approximately $2.07 million and $3.44 million, respectively. Moving that volume by water could also eliminate approximately 5,100 truck trips and reduce associated carbon emissions by roughly 87%. Other potential savings include $4.50 per ton for grain shipments, $1.80 for liquid bulk and $19.10 for salt. The figures represent modeled transportation savings rather than guaranteed commercial returns. “Northwest Indiana is home to some of the nation's largest steel producers, and giving them more ways to reach their customers is critical to their success,” said Ryan McCoy, Ports of Indiana–Burns Harbor Port Director. Infrastructure and Commercial Challenges The report identifies several obstacles to expanded cross-system shipping, including limited shipper awareness, established truck and rail relationships, bridge clearance restrictions, aging locks, seasonal navigation constraints and availability of suitable barges. A BNSF railroad bridge near Lemont, Illinois, was identified as a particular operational bottleneck, while lock closures and restrictions on barge movements can undermine service reliability. The study recommends 15 actions covering market development, industry partnerships, regulatory coordination and infrastructure improvements, including expanding lake-capable barge capacity and improving terminal information available to shippers. “By better connecting these systems, we can expand reliable and cost-effective transportation options, strengthen domestic commerce, and create growth opportunities for American industry and workers across America's Heartland,” said Mike McCoshen, Administrator of the Great Lakes St. Lawrence Seaway Development Corporation. AGLPA and its partners intend to use the findings to engage shippers, carriers and terminal operators in developing commercially viable freight movements. The central conclusion: significant opportunities exist without constructing new waterway connections, provided industry can better utilize those already in place. articles.summary: All 19 crewmembers of a StealthGas LPG carrier have been rescued after the vessel was caught up in a suspected drone attack off Bulgaria, the second serious merchant shipping incident in the western Black Sea in less than 24 hours. articles.body: Europe Gas Operations StealthGas crew airlifted from stricken LPG carrier off Bulgaria Adis Ajdin November 17, 2026 0 226 1 minute read Bulgarian Ministry of Transport Bulgarian Ministry of Transport All 19 crewmembers of a StealthGas LPG carrier have been rescued after the vessel was caught up in a suspected drone attack off Bulgaria, the second serious merchant shipping incident in the western Black Sea in less than 24 hours. The Liberia-flagged, 7,500 cu m Gas Husky got into trouble overnight on Monday while sailing from Alexandria, Egypt, towards Romania’s Midia port. The 2012-built vessel disappeared from tracking systems shortly after midnight, with its emergency position-indicating radio beacon activated around 8 am local time on Tuesday. Bulgarian authorities launched a search and rescue operation around 50 nautical miles east of Byala, deploying military aircraft and a Cougar helicopter after locating a life raft carrying the crew. All 19 Filipino seafarers were evacuated to the Chaika naval airbase near Varna. Two were taken to hospital with minor injuries, while the remaining crew were reported to be in good condition. The vessel was initially reported to have sunk, but Bulgarian officials subsequently indicated that it remained afloat, listing heavily to starboard. Romanian maritime authorities have reported a possible drone strike, although Bulgarian officials have yet to confirm the cause of the casualty. The Gas Husky, owned by Octopus Gas and managed by Greek shipping group Stealth Maritime, was built at Japan’s Kanrei Shipbuilding. The 7,218 dwt fully pressurised LPG carrier forms part of Harry Vafias-led StealthGas’s fleet. The ship was approximately 14.5 nautical miles from the location where the Somali-flagged general cargo vessel Betul 8 capsized on Monday. That vessel, carrying around 3,000 tonnes of wheat from Romania to Egypt, was reportedly struck by two unmanned surface vessels before taking on water. All 12 crewmembers were rescued in an operation involving Bulgarian, Romanian and Turkish forces. The incidents come amid a sharp escalation in attacks on commercial shipping in the western Black Sea. Maritime security consultancy Diaplous has recorded at least 17 merchant vessels attacked off Romania and Bulgaria since mid-July, with several casualties reported in recent weeks. The latest incidents have occurred close to shipping routes used by vessels trading to and from Ukrainian and Romanian Black Sea ports. An Indian seafarer is missing and two others have been hospitalized after the Panama-flagged LPG tanker TARA GAS came under repeated attack in the Strait of Hormuz, forcing its 25-member crew to abandon ship. India’s Ministry of External Affairs said Tuesday that 21 of the 24 Indian nationals aboard had been safely evacuated ashore at Khasab, Oman, while two injured Indian crew members were admitted to a hospital. Search and rescue operations were continuing for the missing seafarer. The latest developments follow two tanker attacks reported Monday by UK Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) , both of which resulted in engine-room fires. According to UKMTO Warning 208-26 , a tanker was attacked at approximately 1900 UTC on November 16, about seven nautical miles north of Khasab, Oman. The attack disabled the vessel and sparked an engine-room fire. The crew was initially reported safe. However, in an update issued Tuesday, UKMTO said a maritime security agency had reported a second strike against the vessel, causing another fire. At that time, the agency said the crew’s whereabouts were unaccounted for. India’s Minister of Ports, Shipping and Waterways, Sarbananda Sonowal, subsequently identified the vessel as TARA GAS , saying it had been targeted in a missile attack on November 16. In a subsequent statement , Sonowal confirmed that the tanker had suffered another attack and its entire crew had abandoned the vessel. “While 24 crew members have been safely accounted for, one Indian seafarer remains missing,” Sonowal said. Video circulating on social media purportedly shows a tanker engulfed in flames near the Strait of Hormuz, although gCaptain has not independently verified the footage. The Indian Embassy in Muscat said it was coordinating with Omani authorities on rescue operations and assistance to the surviving crew. That incident, recorded under UKMTO Warning 207-26 at 0558 UTC, also caused an engine-room fire. All crew members were accounted for, with no casualties initially reported. The attacks underscore the continuing dangers facing commercial shipping in the strategic waterway, where vessel movements remain severely disrupted by the conflict with Iran. articles.summary: The Saab-led MANGROVE consortium has successfully completed Phase 1 Of the Allied Underwater Battlespace Mission Network (AUWB -MN), delivering a milestone in NATO's ambition to establish a secure, interoperable and resilient mission network…
articles.body: MANGROVE Consortium Completes Phase 1 of Allied Underwater Battlespace Mission Network Maritime Activity Reports, Inc. November 17, 2026 © Saab UK The Saab-led MANGROVE consortium has successfully completed Phase 1 Of the Allied Underwater Battlespace Mission Network (AUWB -MN), delivering a milestone in NATO's ambition to establish a secure, interoperable and resilient mission network for underwater battlespace. Bringing together expertise from industry, academia and defense specialists from around the world, the MANGROVE consortium has spent the past year developing the architectural, technical and governance foundations required to enable future multinational underwater battlespace operations. As the strategic importance of the underwater domain grows, the ability to seamlessly and securely integrate crewed and uncrewed systems and maintain situational awareness across multinational operations has become increasingly vital. AUWB-MN is designed to allow nations to share information, coordinate assets and operate as an integrated force regardless of the technology being used. Rather than relying on bespoke integrations between individual systems, AUWB-MN defines common standards and security principles that will allow systems to integrate more rapidly and effectively. This first phase also established the foundations for a future Test and Reference Environment that will form the basis for the next stage of the project, supporting future experimentation, capability development, compliance assessment and operational exercises. The MANGROVE consortium is led by Saab's business area Naval, with CETENA and IDS of the Fincantieri Group, FlySight, GraalTech, Miraya, Saab UK, S2IX and the University of Plymouth.

The company presented its long-term strategy during its Investor Day at the New York Stock Exchange on 16 November 2026. The event focused on GXO’s growth priorities, financial performance and capital allocation plans. GXO is targeting annual organic revenue growth of more than 7% between 2027 and 2030. It also aims to achieve an adjusted EBITA margin above 6.5% by 2030. In addition, the company has set a free cash flow conversion target of 40% to 50% of adjusted EBITDA. The targets reflect GXO’s plans to expand its logistics services while improving operating efficiency. Meanwhile, it is targeting an adjusted EBITDA margin above 7.1% and an adjusted EBITA margin exceeding 4.5%. According to GXO, the targets follow changes to its operating model and commercial strategy over the past year. The company is also focusing on technology, automation and artificial intelligence as part of its long-term development. “Our ambition is to lead the future of supply chain services in the next era of intelligent, AI-powered logistics and solve increasingly complex challenges for customers,” said Patrick Kelleher, CEO, GXO Logistics. Kelleher added that GXO has strengthened its business model and commercial approach while expanding its focus on advanced logistics technology. The financial targets come as the company continues investing in automation across its global warehouse network. GXO recently announced an expanded partnership with Apptronik to test humanoid robots in warehouse operations. The companies are exploring a potential deployment of up to 1,000 robots over the next four years, subject to successful trials and operational requirements. The initiative forms part of GXO’s broader efforts to integrate advanced robotics into logistics operations. GXO currently operates more than 1,000 facilities worldwide, covering over 200 million square feet of logistics space. The company employs more than 150,000 people and provides contract logistics services to customers across multiple industries. November 17, 2026 Image: Riverside | Maritime Matters: The Marinelink Podcast Artificial Intelligence (AI) is a game-changer in various industries, and the maritime sector is no exception. In a recent conversation with Roger Holm, President Marine, Wärtsilä & Siri-Anne Mjåtvedt, CEO, Utkilen, we explored how AI is being integrated into maritime operations to enhance efficiency and safety. This podcast post delves into their insights and experiences, highlighting how AI is not just a trend but a transformative technology for the maritime world. The Evolution of AI in Maritime: A New Paradigm The maritime industry has always been at the forefront of adopting new technologies. Roger Holm emphasized that AI is reshaping how businesses operate by enhancing human decision-making rather than replacing it. He stated, "The real value of AI is strengthening human decision-making. It's about integrating people using AI and data in a more optimized way." This perspective shifts the narrative around AI from being a replacement for human jobs to a tool that empowers maritime professionals to make better, data-driven decisions. For instance, AI can optimize voyage planning and predictive maintenance, ensuring vessels operate at peak efficiency. Utkilen’s Practical Approach to AI Implementation Siri-Anne Mjåtvedt shared how Utkilen adopts a practical approach to AI, treating it as a business tool rather than just a technological project. By providing employees with tools like Microsoft Copilot, the company fosters an environment where everyone can learn and work with AI from day one. Mjåtvedt noted, "If AI improves safety, efficiency, or decision-making, we move forward. If not, we don't." This deliberate evaluation process has led to the implementation of AI-supported solutions that enhance emergency response systems and automate data collection for vessel positioning. These applications not only improve operational efficiency but also allow crew members to focus on high-value tasks, ultimately benefiting customers and the business. The Interconnection of AI, Data, and Decarbonization AI's role in maritime extends beyond operational efficiency; it is also a key player in the industry's decarbonization efforts. Roger highlighted that Wärtsilä invests significantly in research and development to combine AI with decarbonization strategies. With 329 million euros allocated to R&D last year alone, Wärtsilä is committed to finding innovative solutions that align with environmental goals. The integration of AI allows companies to analyze vast amounts of data, turning complex information into actionable insights that support compliance with environmental regulations and improve reliability. Holm pointed out, "By combining AI with domain expertise, we can create more certainty for our customers, ensuring better uptime and operational performance." Key Takeaways: Embracing AI for a Sustainable Future The discussion between Roger Holm and Siri-Anne Mjåtvedt reveals that AI is not merely a buzzword in the maritime industry; it is a vital component of modern operations. Here are the key takeaways: **AI Enhances Decision-Making** : By integrating AI into operations, maritime professionals can make more informed decisions, leading to improved efficiency and safety. **Practical Implementation is Key** : Companies like Utkilen demonstrate the importance of treating AI as a business tool, focusing on its practical applications rather than just technological advancements. **AI Supports Decarbonization** : The maritime industry can leverage AI to meet environmental goals, optimize operations, and ensure compliance with regulations. In conclusion, as the maritime industry continues to evolve, embracing AI will be crucial for companies looking to enhance their operations and contribute to a sustainable future. The insights from leaders like Roger Holm and Siri-Anne Mjåtvedt serve as a guiding light for maritime professionals navigating this transformative landscape. articles.title: Interferry2026: Global Ferry Leaders Convened in Bangkok for 50th Annual Conference
articles.summary: The global ferry industry convened on the banks of the Chao Phraya River in Bangkok, Thailand, for the 50th annual Interferry conference. Half a century after its founding, the trade association brought together executives from major ferry groups…
articles.body: Interferry2026: Global Ferry Leaders Convened in Bangkok for 50th Annual Conference Maritime Activity Reports, Inc. November 17, 2026 Image courtesy Interferry Image courtesy Interferry The global ferry industry convened on the banks of the Chao Phraya River in Bangkok, Thailand, for the 50th annual Interferry conference. Half a century after its founding, the trade association brought together executives from major ferry groups, regional operators, and technology providers to discuss changes in how ferries are powered, crewed, and operated. Over five decades, Interferry has evolved from an informal meeting of ferry operators into an international trade association that gives passenger and vehicle ferry operators a common voice. In Bangkok, more than 400 delegates representing major groups, family-owned enterprises, and public transit authorities attended the conference, which ran from October 31 to November 4. Discussions covered how to cut emissions, recruit seafarers, improve domestic ferry safety in developing countries, and maintain the services that isolated communities depend on. Shore Power: Who Pays for It Decarbonization dominated discussions throughout the event. While ferry shipowners continue investing millions of dollars in battery-electric ships, hybrid systems, and vessels designed to run on alternative fuels, industry leaders warned that ports and local power grids also need investment if electric ferries are to charge between sailings. Niclas Mårtensson, CEO of Stena Line , said the limits of local power grids were a problem ferry operators could not solve on their own. “Ferry operators are committing massive multi-digit million capital investments directly into zero- and low-emission vessels, but shipowners cannot solve onshore infrastructure challenges,” Mårtensson said. “Achieving meaningful decarbonization requires true partnerships with and financial commitment by national governments and regional port authorities to build high-capacity shore power and charging networks.” Panos Dikaios, CEO of Greece’s Attica Group, also stressed that the switch to electric propulsion depends on whether local grids can supply enough power and whether government policies support the necessary investment. Image courtesy Interferry Retaining Crew, Adapting to Gen Z As the maritime industry faces a global shortage of qualified seafarers, a ferry leaders panel examined what a career on ferries can offer compared with working on deep-sea ships. Guido Grimaldi, corporate commercial director of the Grimaldi Group , said operators should make those differences clearer when recruiting. “Unlike deep-sea maritime careers that take crew away from home for months at a time, ferry shipping offers predictable rotation schedules, structured shoreside life, and a real balance between family and career,” Grimaldi noted. “We have to be far more proactive and explicit in demonstrating these career pathways to the next generation of maritime professionals.” Katy Taylor, CEO of Wightlink , looked at what younger recruits expect from their employers, from the technology they use at work to the opportunities they have to advance. “We are competing for talent in a completely altered job market,” Taylor argued. “Adapting our culture, technology, and career growth structures to meet the expectations of Gen Z is not an optional human resources strategy - there simply is no other choice if we intend to remain operational.” Image courtesy Interferry Keeping Lifeline Services Viable The conference also heard from smaller ferry operators that provide lifeline services to islands and remote communities, where even a state-subsidized public service contract leaves operators with costs to manage and revenue to earn. Operators described how they balance those demands with the needs of passengers who rely on the ferry. Good food on board can bring in extra revenue, while helping passengers during severe weather or family emergencies can strengthen an operator’s relationship with the community it serves. FerrySafe’s work in Lagos The conference reviewed Interferry’s work on domestic ferry safety through its ongoing FerrySafe initiative. A dedicated session focused on the association’s partnership with the Lagos State Waterways Authority (LASWA) in Nigeria. Akpan Ukeme Sunday, head of LASWA’s Vessel Survey and Standards Department , described what the training, mentoring, and engine system checks mean for ferry operations in Lagos. “The structured technical training, mentorship, and engine system auditing provided through our partnership with Interferry is delivering immediate, practical changes on the water in Lagos,” he said. “This direct transfer of expertise is actively building a safer, more resilient water transport network for millions of daily commuters.” Image courtesy Interferry From Bangkok to the Åland Islands At the conference, host and outgoing Interferry president Supapan Pichaironarongsongkram, chairwoman of Chao Phraya Express Boat , handed over the Interferry presidency to Marcus Risberg, CEO of Viking Line , which will host Interferry2027, the 51st annual Interferry conference in Mariehamn, Åland Islands. “Moving from the metropolis of Bangkok to the small, maritime-steeped archipelago of the Åland Islands will certainly offer a distinct change of setting,” remarked Risberg. “Yet the Åland Islands sits right at the geographic and operational heart of Baltic Sea shipping. We look forward to welcoming the global industry to our historic island home.” In his closing remarks, Interferry CEO Mike Corrigan reflected on what has kept ferry operators coming together for five decades. “For fifty years, this association has proven that our industry accomplishes more when we work together,” Corrigan concluded. “Interferry annual conferences have always felt less like standard trade events and more like a family reunion of dedicated professionals. As we tackle decarbonization, safety, and workforce evolution, Bangkok has shown that we are remarkably well-equipped for the next 50 years – because we are truly stronger together.”

The agreement covers engineering, procurement, fabrication, and installation of the substation, which will form part of the wind farm’s electricity transmission infrastructure. Semco Maritime will handle engineering, procurement, and installation of the electrical systems, while PTSC will manufacture the substation’s structural components. The project is located approximately 40 km offshore Taichung and is being developed by Copenhagen Offshore Partners on behalf of CIP’s sixth flagship fund. CIP is targeting financial close by the end of the second quarter of 2027, with grid connection scheduled for 2030. The latest agreement marks the second collaboration between the three companies in Taiwan, following their work on the 495 MW Fengmiao I offshore wind farm. For the first development, Semco Maritime and PTSC delivered a 3,400-tonne topside and an 8,000-tonne jacket for the offshore substation. The facility was installed offshore in August this year and energised in October, while construction of the wider Fengmiao I development continues. Fengmiao II secured its development allocation in Taiwan’s offshore wind Round 3.2 auction in August 2024. The latest award represents another major construction package for the project ahead of its planned financing milestone. articles.title: Allseas taps Aker Solutions for recycling of 50,000-ton North Sea platform topside
articles.summary: Five decades after a North Sea platform was built, Aker Solutions has been selected to handle the dismantling and recycling of its topside.
articles.body: Project & Tenders November 17, 2026 · 43 minutes ago Allseas taps Aker Solutions for recycling of 50,000-ton North Sea platform topside Five decades after a North Sea platform was built, Aker Solutions has been selected to handle the dismantling and recycling of its topside. MC Melisa Cavcic Senior Editor 2 minutes read LinkedIn X Email Statfjord A platform in the North Sea Source: Harald Pettersen/Equinor Norway-based energy services provider Aker Solutions has been picked to oversee the final chapter of a 50,000-ton topside from a North Sea offshore platform, taking on its dismantling and recycling in a project that will bring the structure back to the Stord yard, where it was originally built in the 1970s. While announcing a letter of intent (LOI) from Allseas for the reception, dismantling, and recycling of the topside from Equinor's Statfjord A platform in the North Sea, Aker Solutions explained that the platform was originally built at Stord in 1975 and prepared for installation on the concrete gravity base structure in 1976. This platform has been an important contributor to production from the Statfjord field , one of the largest oil fields ever developed in the North Sea. As the original builder of the topside, Aker Solutions elaborates it has detailed knowledge of the structure and extensive experience in maintenance, modification, and life-extension work carried out over several decades. The structure will now return to the yard to complete its life cycle. The LOI for a contract, worth between NOK 0.5 billion ($52 million) and NOK 1.5 billion ($155 million), covers disposal-related preparatory work, reception, dismantling, and recycling of the approximately 50,000-ton topside following offshore removal by Allseas' Pioneering Spirit heavy-lift vessel. Related Articles Decommissioning Allseas books ABL for 60,000-ton topside single-lift ops in next North Sea decom chapter 2 min read " Statfjord A has played an important role in Norway's energy history for almost half a century. We are proud that Allseas and end-client Equinor have selected Aker Solutions to handle the final phase of the topside’s life cycle. The award confirms the strong position we have built in decommissioning and recycling through decades of efficient project execution. " — Guro Rausand Executive Vice President for New Build at Aker Solutions Statfjord A is expected to arrive at Aker Solutions' decommissioning facility at Stord between 2029 and 2031. The dismantling and recycling campaign is expected to take approximately two years. At peak, the project is anticipated to involve around 100 personnel at the Stord yard. " Our decommissioning team has extensive experience in complex offshore decommissioning projects. Combined with our specialized decommissioning facility at Stord, this gives us a strong foundation for carrying out the work safely, efficiently and with a high degree of material recovery. " — Rausand added. The LOI comes shortly after Aker Solutions landed a deal with PTSC Mechanical and Construction Limited Company (PTSC M&C) to handle the multimillion-dollar modernization of an oil field off the coast of Qatar. The award follows another contract, involving a three-year charter of the Skandi Seven for deepwater construction and subsea maintenance work offshore Africa. articles.body: Europe Offshore Allseas taps Aker Solutions for massive topside dismantling job Bojan Lepic November 17, 2026 0 594 1 minute read Equinor Equinor Norwegian offshore engineering group Aker Solutions has received a letter of intent from Allseas to dismantle and recycle Equinor’s Statfjord A platform topside in the North Sea. The agreement covers preparatory work, reception, dismantling and recycling of the approximately 50,000-tonne structure at Aker Solutions’ Stord facility in western Norway. Classified as sizeable by Aker Solutions, the contract is valued at between NOK500m and NOK1.5bn ($52m to $155m). The company expects to book the Statfjord A contract in the fourth quarter of 2026, subject to a final award. Allseas will remove the topside using its heavy-lift vessel Pioneering Spirit, which will lift the structure from its concrete gravity-based foundation in a single operation. The topside is expected to arrive at Stord between 2029 and 2031, with dismantling and recycling taking approximately two years. Around 100 personnel are expected to work on the project during peak activity. Originally constructed at Stord in the 1970s, Statfjord A began production in November 1979 and has undergone several life extensions. Equinor and Allseas first announced arrangements for removing and recycling the structure in 2019, with Kvaerner, subsequently integrated into Aker Solutions, selected for the onshore work. More recently, Allseas appointed consultancy ABL as marine warranty surveyor for the removal campaign. The project will use Pioneering Spirit’s upgraded lifting system, now rated at 60,000 tonnes. Aker Solutions previously worked with Allseas on the decommissioning of the Gyda platform, whose 18,000-tonne topside was delivered to Stord for recycling in 2022.
