articles.title: Fourth floating LNG terminal put into operation mode to fuel Germany’s energy security
articles.summary: Germany’s federally commissioned LNG terminal program is now complete, with four floating LNG terminals delivered in just four years.
articles.body: Vessels November 17, 2026 · 6 minutes ago Fourth floating LNG terminal put into operation mode to fuel Germany’s energy security Germany’s federally commissioned LNG terminal program is now complete, with four floating LNG terminals delivered in just four years. MC Melisa Cavcic Senior Editor 1 minutes read LinkedIn X Email Energos Force Source: DET In another step towards diversifying Germany's energy network to curb dependence on individual gas suppliers and transport routes, Deutsche Energy Terminal (DET), part of the German Federal Ministry for Economic Affairs and Climate Action and a state-owned operator of four liquefied natural gas (LNG) terminals, has strengthened the country’s gas import flexibility and security of supply by commissioning its fourth and final federally commissioned terminal in Stade. Germany’s newly commissioned LNG terminal in Stade is expected to feed up to 3.2 billion cubic meters of natural gas into the national grid in 2027, which is equivalent, in theoretical annual heating demand, to around 2.6 million four-person households. The FSRU Energos Force will receive LNG from LNG carriers, regasify it on board, and feed it into the German gas grid. " With the LNG terminal in Stade, we are strengthening Germany’s energy supply and making it more independent and more resilient. In a challenging time, Lower Saxony took on responsibility and made an important contribution to putting the energy supply on a broader footing. Security of supply is the prerequisite for economic strength. At the same time, we are looking ahead: we need an energy infrastructure that provides security today and paves the way to a climate-neutral energy supply tomorrow. Stade is an important location for this. " — Olaf Lies Minister-President of the State of Lower Saxony Related Articles Fossil Energy Boost for Germany’s energy security comes with third LNG terminal up and running 4 min read The commissioning marks the completion of the country’s four-terminal floating LNG program, delivered by DET in four years, diversifying gas import routes. Aside from the new Stade site , Deutsche Energy Terminal operates two LNG terminals in Wilhelmshaven and one in Brunsbüttel . " With the LNG terminal in Stade, we are commissioning the fourth and final federally owned terminal. Four terminals in less than four years: this shows how quickly Germany can act when it matters. We have put our gas supply on a broader footing and are thus more independent of individual suppliers and transport routes. With the Energos Force, another import route is now being added that will strengthen our supply this winter already. In 2027, up to 3.2 billion cubic meters of natural gas are expected to be fed into the German gas grid via the Stade terminal. In theory, this corresponds to the annual heating energy demand of around 2.6 million four-person households. " — Katherina Reiche Federal Minister for Economic Affairs and Energy Related Articles Clean Fuel FSRU docks in Stade as LNG terminal prepares to feed gas into German grid from November 3 min read According to DET, these four terminals strengthen Germany’s security of supply and create additional options for importing natural gas independently of individual transport routes and supply structures. " Realizing and commissioning four floating LNG terminals within four years was an extraordinary task and a joint effort by many parties. Having originally planned, permitted and built at several locations at once in an acute emergency, we now have, with the commissioning of the Stade site, four terminals for a secure and resilient energy supply for Germany. articles.summary: US energy company Apache said that production from its UK North Sea assets remains unaffected despite escalating industrial action involving around 170 offshore workers. articles.body: Europe Offshore Apache keeps North Sea assets producing despite worker walkouts Bojan Lepic November 17, 2026 0 522 1 minute read Apache Apache US energy company Apache said that production from its UK North Sea assets remains unaffected despite escalating industrial action involving around 170 offshore workers. Members of the Unite union staged a series of rolling strikes across seven Apache-operated installations over the weekend as part of an ongoing dispute concerning pay and working conditions. Workers on Forties Alpha, Forties Bravo, Forties Delta, and Beryl Bravo walked out on November 13, followed by employees on Forties Charlie, Forties Echo, and Beryl Alpha on November 15. The latest action ended on Monday morning, with union members also staging a protest outside Apache’s Aberdeen headquarters. Unite claimed the action was disrupting offshore operations and accused the company of imposing below-inflation pay increases and maintaining an unfair seven-day clawback policy. Apache rejected the suggestion that production was affected, saying 49% of bargaining unit employees scheduled to work reported for duty during the strikes. The company said all its producing assets remained online and that neither the Forties Pipeline System nor the SAGE gas pipeline had been disrupted. Beryl Bravo was the only installation offline, although the platform is already undergoing decommissioning. Apache said its pay offer remained available and that it had invited UK conciliation service Acas to help resolve the dispute. The company previously offered workers a 4% pay increase, which Unite rejected. The strikes come as Apache prepares to end production from its UK North Sea assets by 2029, followed by the decommissioning of seven platforms and approximately 260 wells across the Forties and Beryl fields. articles.title: Shell kicks off gas production from its deepwater project in Southeast Asia
articles.summary: Shell has brought online a natural gas development off the coast of Malaysia, which is home to an offshore platform designed to run on solar energy.
articles.body: Exploration & Production November 17, 2026 · 2 minutes ago Shell kicks off gas production from its deepwater project in Southeast Asia Shell has brought online a natural gas development off the coast of Malaysia, which is home to an offshore platform designed to run on solar energy. MC Melisa Cavcic Senior Editor 2 minutes read LinkedIn X Email Rosmari-Marjoram topside sailaway Source: Malaysia Marine and Heavy Engineering Holdings (MHB) Sarawak Shell, a subsidiary of the UK-headquartered energy giant Shell, has begun flowing the first gas from its deepwater fields off Sarawak, Malaysia, which are expected to support the company's production growth into the 2030s. Shell has started production from the Rosmari and Marjoram fields located 220 kilometers off the coast of Sarawak, bringing its latest development on stream four years after making a final investment decision (FID) in 2022 to develop the project, containing these deepwater sour gas fields discovered in 2014. " Shell is proud of its long and successful history in Malaysia. We have strong expertise in this basin, and the start-up of Rosmari-Marjoram contributes to production growth into the 2030s. This project builds on decades of experience to bring new gas supply online efficiently and competitively. " — Peter Costello President of Upstream The company explains that the gas produced from Rosmari-Marjoram will be piped to a new onshore gas plant in Bintulu, Sarawak, where it will be processed and fed to the Petronas LNG Complex . The development consists of a subsea tie-back, an unmanned wellhead platform, a 207-kilometer pipeline to shore, and an onshore gas plant at Bintulu. The project’s offshore platform is powered by solar panels , with back-up diesel generators available when needed. The onshore plant draws on the predominantly hydropower-based local electricity grid, supplemented by renewable energy certificates to achieve 100% renewable power. Related Articles Fossil Energy Shell’s new solar-powered platform with 20-year design life on its way to offshore gas field (Gallery) 2 min read " The offshore platform is designed to be powered by solar panels when it is unmanned, with batteries providing storage for up to three days of electricity. Diesel generators provide a backup source of electricity and help to power the platform when personnel visit for maintenance, which requires more energy to run ancillary services. The onshore gas plant is run on the equivalent of 100% hydropower, with renewable energy certificates complementing hydropower used directly from the electricity grid. " — Shell elaborated. The firm drilled Malaysia’s first oil well in 1910 and has been producing gas offshore since 1982. In addition to Rosmari-Marjoram, the company has interests in multiple producing fields off the coast of Sarawak, including Timi and Gorek , and is exploring other potential opportunities in the basin. articles.summary: A growing group of African nations is pushing ahead with plans to introduce carbon charges on international shipping, raising the prospect of another regional emissions regime for shipowners already grappling with European environmental legislation. articles.body: Africa Environment Regulatory African nations join forces to impose carbon charges on shipping Sam Chambers November 17, 2026 0 1,686 1 minute read Norden Norden A growing group of African nations is pushing ahead with plans to introduce carbon charges on international shipping, raising the prospect of another regional emissions regime for shipowners already grappling with European environmental legislation. Guinea, Ivory Coast and Mauritania have signed an agreement at the COP31 climate summit in Antalya, Turkey, to develop a coordinated approach to charging ships for their carbon emissions. The initiative, promoted by the Africa Sovereign Carbon Registry Foundation (ASCRF), builds on existing schemes in Djibouti and Gabon, with the ambition of establishing a continent-wide framework for raising climate finance from international shipping and aviation. Under the model pioneered by Djibouti, vessels are charged $17 per tonne of CO2 calculated on 50% of emissions from voyages to and from the country’s ports. Gabon has adopted a similar approach, increasing its own carbon charge in September. The revenues are intended to support national climate adaptation and energy transition projects. The latest agreement brings the number of countries associated with the proposed African coalition to six, although the status of Liberia’s involvement remains contentious. Monrovia stated earlier this year that it would not impose a unilateral carbon levy on international shipping. Other African countries are considering similar schemes. The development comes at a particularly sensitive moment for shipping’s decarbonisation negotiations, with the International Maritime Organization due to resume discussions on its proposed global emissions framework later this month. Unlike the EU Emissions Trading System, the African arrangements currently in force impose fixed charges rather than requiring companies to purchase tradable emissions allowances. No implementation dates or final charging arrangements have been announced for the three newest participating countries. articles.title: China emerges as dry bulk export powerhouse
articles.summary: China’s transformation from the world’s dominant dry bulk importer into an increasingly significant exporter is gathering pace, with outbound cargo volumes more than doubling since 2020 and accounting for nearly two-thirds of global dry bulk shipment growth this year. articles.body: Dry Cargo Greater China China emerges as dry bulk export powerhouse Sam Chambers November 17, 2026 0 1,410 1 minute read China’s transformation from the world’s dominant dry bulk importer into an increasingly significant exporter is gathering pace, with outbound cargo volumes more than doubling since 2020 and accounting for nearly two-thirds of global dry bulk shipment growth this year. New analysis from Ursa Shipbrokers, using Signal Ocean vessel-tracking data, shows Chinese dry bulk loadings reached 274.9m tonnes in the first 10 months of 2026, up 14.9% year-on-year China accounted for 35.6m tonnes of the 54.4m-tonne increase in global dry bulk loadings during the period, an extraordinary contribution from a country traditionally viewed principally as a destination for raw materials. Its share of worldwide dry bulk loadings has climbed from just 2.5% in 2020 to 5.5% this year, with annual export shipments rising from 128.6m tonnes to 291.5m tonnes between 2020 and 2025. September set a new monthly record of 32.8m tonnes, while October’s 29.5m tonnes remained 12.8% above the corresponding month last year. The changing trade patterns are particularly significant for owners of handysize, supramax and ultramax vessels, which transport many of China’s outbound industrial commodities. The shift has not escaped the attention of leading dry bulk owners. “From being an almost sole importer of dry cargoes [China] has emerged into a large exporter over the last few years, a very interesting development indeed,” Ivar Hansson Myklebust, chairman and chief executive of Norwegian owner Belships, told Splash in an interview last week. China’s struggling property market has contributed to the change, with excess domestic production finding buyers overseas. Cement and clinker exports have climbed from negligible levels to around 25m tonnes in just a few years. Steel remains another major export commodity. Chinese customs figures show 95.5m tonnes of steel products were shipped overseas between January and October, although that represented a 2.3% decline from the corresponding period last year. BRS Shipbrokers recently reported an 18.5% increase in Chinese dry bulk export cargoes during the first nine months of 2026, reinforcing the broader trend identified by Ursa. The export boom is unfolding despite weakness in China’s domestic manufacturing economy, with October’s purchasing managers’ index slipping back into contraction territory.
